Features.title: Everything visitors expect from an accessibility menu
Features.description: And what you need to ship it: your brand, your languages, a strict CSP and no tracking.

items.title: Accessible itself
items.text: The panel is a WAI-ARIA dialog with a focus trap, and the page behind it is inert. Switches, radio groups and sections work with the keyboard and screen readers, in Windows High Contrast and with reduced motion.

items.title: Your brand, your logo
items.text: Set theme.primary and the launcher, header and active states follow. Change colors, radius, font and the launcher's logo, from JavaScript or with CSS variables.

items.title: 23 adjustments, 7 profiles
items.text: Text size, spacing, contrast, saturation, reading line, focus window, read mode, stopping animations and more, plus quick profiles that switch on a few at once.

items.title: Arabic and RTL
items.text: English and Arabic built in, and you can add your own. The panel mirrors right to left and starts in the page's language.

items.title: Any website
items.text: Plain HTML, WordPress, React, Next.js, Vue, Angular, Svelte, Astro. Safe with server rendering, and it re-attaches when a page swaps its body.

items.title: Small, no dependencies
items.text: About 23 KB gzipped. Adjustments are classes and CSS variables on html, and destroy() removes every one of them.

items.title: Strict CSP, Trusted Types
items.text: No eval, no innerHTML, no inline scripts. Pass a nonce for its style tags and it runs under a strict Content Security Policy.

items.title: Private by default
items.text: No network requests, no cookies, no analytics. Preferences stay in the visitor's browser, and persist: false stores nothing at all.

Honest.title: A preferences menu, not a compliance tool
Honest.description: Accessibility overlays are often sold as a fix for lawsuits. This widget isn't one, and it doesn't pretend to be.
is: A menu that lets each visitor change text size, spacing, colors, motion and reading aids on your pages.
A small, open-source script that runs only in the browser and stores preferences only there.
Accessible itself: tested with axe-core and keyboard-only scripts in every release.
A convenience to offer on top of an accessible site.
isNot: It doesn't make a website ADA, EAA, EN 301 549 or WCAG compliant.
It doesn't scan, repair or rewrite your markup: missing alt text, labels and contrast still need fixing at the source.
It isn't a legal defence, and it shouldn't be advertised as one.
It doesn't replace testing with real users and assistive technology.

Footer.about: A free, open-source accessibility preferences menu for any website. MIT licensed, no dependencies, no tracking.

Hero.title: Let every visitor adjust your site to their needs
Hero.sub: A free accessibility preferences menu for any website: text size, contrast, spacing, reading aids and motion, in English and Arabic. No dependencies, no tracking, about 24 KB.
Hero.shortcut: Or press Alt + A on any page of this site.

Install.title: Getting started
Install.description: Install the package, add the widget to your pages and give it your brand color. It takes a few minutes.

install.title: Install
install.text: Use your package manager, or load one script from a CDN with no build step. The CDN tag pins an exact version with its integrity hash.

add.title: Add it to your pages
add.text: Call init() once, in the browser, after the page loads. It mounts the launcher on body and returns the widget. In React and Next.js, render the component in your root layout instead.

customize.title: Make it yours
customize.text: Every option is optional. Pass your brand color, the side of the screen, your logo and a starting language, and remove the controls you don't want to offer.

statement.title: Link your accessibility statement
statement.text: If your site has an accessibility statement, link it from the panel's footer. Only http, https and relative URLs are accepted.

Install.frameworkText: Using Vue, Angular, Svelte, Astro or a CMS? <link>See the setup for your framework</link>
Install.customizeMore: Every option is listed in the <link>API reference</link>
Install.compliance: The widget lets visitors adjust your pages. It doesn't make a site compliant with ADA, EAA, EN 301 549 or WCAG: that depends on your own markup. <link>Read the limitations</link>
Install.privacy: No network requests and no cookies. Preferences are saved in the visitor's localStorage unless you pass persist: false. Privacy and storage

Api.title: API reference
Api.description: Every option, theme key, method and export of the package, with its type and default.

options.title: Options
options.description: Passed to init(options), as props of AccessibilityWidget, or later to widget.setOptions(options).

theme.title: Theme
theme.description: The keys of the theme option. Colors take any CSS color; only hex colors are checked for contrast.

methods.title: Instance methods
methods.description: init() returns the widget. The script-tag build exposes the same exports on window.A11yWidget.

react.title: React
react.description: From open-accessibility-widget/react, which also re-exports everything else. The entry is marked "use client".

settings.title: Settings
settings.description: What getSettings() returns, and what setSettings() and initialSettings accept. Percentages use 100 for unchanged; values outside the range are clamped and unknown values dropped.

entries.title: Package contents
entries.description: Each entry ships ESM, CommonJS and type declarations. No runtime dependencies.

options.position: Screen side of the launcher and panel.
options.offset: Distance from the screen edges, in px (0–1000).
options.theme: Colors, radius and font: see Theme below.
options.icon: Launcher logo: an image URL or a DOM element. Pass only trusted elements: they are cloned as they are.
options.logo: Logo next to the panel title.
options.features: Set a control to false to remove it. A removed setting stays off.
options.initialSettings: Settings for visitors with nothing saved.
options.languages: Entries of the language menu, or false to hide the menu.
options.labels: Override single strings on top of the active language.
options.shortcut: Shortcut that opens and closes the panel and brings the widget back after “Hide widget”. With false, the hide button is removed.
options.statementUrl: Link to your accessibility statement in the panel's footer (http, https or relative).
options.showSkipLink: A “Skip to main content” link. Left out when the page has no main or h1, or already starts with its own skip link.
options.persist: Save settings in localStorage, kept in sync across tabs.
options.nonce: CSP nonce for the injected style tags.
options.onChange: Called when the visitor changes something.

theme.primary: Brand color: launcher, header and active states.
theme.onPrimary: Text and icon color on top of primary.
theme.surface: Footer, segmented controls and hover states.
theme.radius: Corner radius: a number in px or any CSS length.

methods.open: Open, close or toggle the panel.
methods.getSettings: The current settings, as a frozen snapshot.
methods.getState: The settings and whether the panel is open.
methods.setSettings: Merge changes: an object, or a function of the previous settings. Input is validated and invalid values are dropped. Setting profiles applies their adjustments too.
methods.toggleProfile: Turn a profile on or off.
methods.reset: Return every adjustment to the page as authored.
methods.setOptions: Change appearance and behaviour options at runtime.
methods.subscribe: Listen to settings and open-state changes. Returns a function that stops listening.
methods.destroy: Remove the widget and undo every change it made to the page.

react.component: Mounts the widget with these options. Changed props call setOptions(); unmounting removes the widget. Renders nothing itself.
react.hook: Read and control the widget from any component. widget is null until it mounts.

exports.init: Mount the widget on body and return it. Calling it again replaces the existing widget.
exports.getAccessibilityWidget: The widget that is running, if any.
exports.onActiveWidgetChange: Listen for a widget being created or destroyed. Returns a function that stops listening.
exports.ranges: Minimum, maximum and step of each percentage setting.
exports.profiles: The profile ids, and the adjustments each profile switches on.
exports.sanitize: Validate untrusted input into complete settings.
exports.languages: English and Arabic, to extend with your own languages.

settings.profiles: Active profiles, in the order they were turned on.
settings.letterSpacing: Letter spacing, in percent (not applied to Arabic).
settings.textMagnifier: Shows the text under the pointer, enlarged.
settings.colors: Custom text, heading and background colors.
settings.media: Mute media, hide images, stop CSS animations.
settings.focus: Strong outline on keyboard focus / on hover.

entries.core: Any framework, or plain JavaScript with a bundler.
entries.react: React component and hook; react 18 or later is an optional peer dependency.
entries.global: Script-tag build, about 23 KB gzipped; exposes window.A11yWidget.

Frameworks.title: Works with your stack
Frameworks.description: One small package for every framework, CMS and plain HTML page. Pick yours for the setup code.
Frameworks.statement: Pass statementUrl to link your accessibility statement from the panel's footer.

vanilla.name: Plain HTML / JavaScript
vanilla.blurb: One script tag and one call, with no build step. Or import it from npm in any bundler.
notes: The script-tag build exposes every export on window.A11yWidget, for example A11yWidget.getAccessibilityWidget()?.open().
Calling init() again replaces the existing widget.
Pages that swap body (Hotwire Turbo, htmx hx-boost) are supported: the widget re-attaches itself and re-applies the visitor's settings.

react.name: React
react.blurb: A component and a hook, for Vite, Remix, Gatsby and any React 18 or 19 app.
notes: The component renders nothing itself: the widget mounts on body.
Changing a prop updates the running widget with setOptions(); unmounting the component removes it.
useAccessibility() returns the current settings, whether the panel is open, and the widget (null until it mounts).

next.name: Next.js
next.blurb: Put the component in your root layout. The React entry is already marked “use client”.
notes: Works in a Server Component layout, with no wrapper of your own.
Nothing runs on the server: the widget starts in the browser after hydration.
With a nonce-based CSP, pass the request's nonce as nonce.
This site is built with Next.js and uses the component in its own root layout.

vue.name: Vue
vue.blurb: Start it in onMounted and remove it in onBeforeUnmount.
notes: Call init() in your root component, so it runs once for the whole app.
With Nuxt, use a client-only plugin instead (see Nuxt).

nuxt.name: Nuxt
nuxt.blurb: A client-only plugin starts the widget once for the whole app.
notes: The .client suffix keeps the plugin out of server rendering.
The widget keeps its state across route changes.

angular.name: Angular
angular.blurb: Start it after the first render, outside the zone.
notes: runOutsideAngular keeps the widget's listeners from running change detection. Zoneless apps don't need it.
With Angular SSR, use afterNextRender or check isPlatformBrowser.

svelte.name: Svelte
svelte.blurb: Start it in onMount in your root layout; the function it returns removes the widget.
notes: In SvelteKit, onMount runs only in the browser.
Put it in the root +layout.svelte so it stays across pages.

astro.name: Astro
astro.blurb: A script in your layout: Astro bundles it and runs it in the browser.
notes: With view transitions, the widget re-attaches itself and re-applies the visitor's settings after each navigation.
Astro bundles script tags, so the import works without a client directive.

cms.name: WordPress and CMS
cms.blurb: Paste one script before the closing body tag: WordPress, Shopify, Webflow, Wix, PHP or Django templates.
notes: Use your theme's footer, a header-and-footer plugin, or your CMS's “custom code” setting.
Keep the integrity attribute: the browser refuses the file if the CDN ever serves anything else.
To theme it without JavaScript, set its CSS variables (see the guide on colors).

Guides.title: Guides
Guides.description: Theming, languages, controls, privacy, security, and what the widget can't do.

theming.title: Colors, logo and placement
theming.summary: Match the widget to your brand: colors, radius, font, logo, side of the screen and size.
theming.intro: The widget brings its own styles and never inherits your site's CSS, so it looks the same on every page. Theme it with options or with CSS variables.

colors.title: Theme colors
colors.text: Pass a theme object. primary colors the launcher, header and active states, and onPrimary is the text and icon color on top of it. Every key is optional.

css.title: CSS variables
css.text: When a CMS or tag manager adds the widget, theme it from CSS. The variables go on .a11yw-widget; --a11yw-hl on :root sets the outline color of the highlight adjustments.

contrast.title: Contrast checks
contrast.text: A console warning tells you when your theme makes part of the widget fail WCAG contrast. Only hex colors are checked.
items: onPrimary on primary: 4.5:1.
primary as the focus outline on background: 3:1.
text and mutedText on background, and footer links on surface: 4.5:1.

logo.title: Logo
logo.text: icon replaces the launcher's icon and logo adds one next to the panel title. Both take an image URL or a DOM element. Pass only elements you trust: they are cloned as they are.

placement.title: Position and size
placement.text: The launcher sits in a bottom corner. When keyboard focus lands on a page control under it, it steps aside until focus moves on (WCAG 2.4.11), but it still covers that corner for mouse and touch users: keep it free, add bottom padding to your page, or move the launcher with offset.

languages.title: Languages and RTL
languages.summary: English and Arabic are built in. Add your own languages, change single strings, or force a direction.
languages.intro: Visitors switch languages from the menu in the panel's header, and the panel's direction follows the language.

choose.title: Starting language
choose.text: The widget starts in the visitor's last choice, otherwise in the page's html lang (so ar-EG gives Arabic, right to left), otherwise in the first language of the list. Pass language to choose it yourself, or languages: false to hide the menu.

custom.title: Add a language
custom.text: Add your own entries next to builtInLanguages. Strings missing from a language fall back to English.

strings.title: Change single strings
strings.text: labels overrides strings on top of whichever language is active. increase, decrease and reset can place the setting's name with '{'label'}'; without it, the name is added at the end. Percentages are formatted for the active language.

rtl.title: Direction
rtl.text: A custom language without dir is shown right to left when its code is a right-to-left language (ar, he, fa, ur…). dir forces one direction for every language.

controls.title: Controls, defaults and profiles
controls.summary: Remove controls you don't offer, set first-visit defaults, and know what each quick profile turns on.
controls.intro: Every visitor sees the full panel unless you remove parts of it, and their own choices always win over your defaults.

remove.title: Remove controls
remove.text: Set a control to false in features to remove it; a removed setting stays off. Every setting can be removed, plus profiles (the whole profile grid) and readMode. A profile card is hidden when all of its adjustments are removed.

defaults.title: First-visit defaults
defaults.text: initialSettings applies to visitors who have nothing saved. Once they change something, their choice is saved and wins. “Reset all” returns to the page as you authored it, not to these defaults.

profiles.title: Quick profiles
profiles.text: Profiles switch on a few adjustments at once. They are not medical tools and don't make a page safe for any condition. Visitors can change every adjustment afterwards, and turning a profile off keeps the ones they changed. The ids are kept for compatibility; the names say what the profiles do.

precedence.title: What wins
items: Your site's styles: what every visitor gets by default.

Operating system and browser settings (prefers-reduced-motion, forced-colors, zoom, default font size): the widget never overrides them and never switches anything on because of them. In forced-colors mode its color filters are off.
initialSettings: your defaults for first-time visitors.
The visitor's saved choices: always win once made.

profiles.name: Motion sensitivity
profiles.watch: GIFs, canvas, video in cross-origin iframes and animation that scripts draw frame by frame are not stopped

profiles.name: Low vision
profiles.watch: The contrast filter changes images too

profiles.name: Focus mode
profiles.on: Focus window, stop animations, low saturation
profiles.watch: The window follows the pointer, a tap and keyboard focus

profiles.name: Easy reading
profiles.on: Highlight headings and links, reading line, readable font
profiles.watch: Outlines add visual noise on busy pages

profiles.name: Quiet media
profiles.watch: Media the visitor starts or unmutes keeps its sound

profiles.name: Comfortable reading
profiles.on: Text 120%, line spacing 130%, readable font, large cursor
profiles.watch: The large cursor replaces the system cursor size

accessibility.title: The widget's own accessibility
accessibility.summary: How the panel works with a keyboard, screen readers, high contrast and reduced motion, and how it is tested.
accessibility.intro: A widget that offers accessibility settings has to be accessible itself. The panel follows WAI-ARIA patterns and is tested in every release.

patterns.title: What assistive technology finds
patterns.text: The panel uses standard roles and states, so screen readers announce it like any other control.
items: The panel is a modal dialog with a focus trap. While it's open, the rest of the page is inert, so screen-reader virtual cursors stay inside. Escape, the close button or a click outside closes it, and focus returns to the launcher.
Sections are an accordion (aria-expanded), toggles are switches (role="switch"), profile cards are toggle buttons (aria-pressed), and segmented choices are radio groups.
Steppers announce the new value with its name (“Text size 120%”) and say when a limit is reached. Resetting is announced too.
The language menu is a select-only combobox with a listbox: arrow keys, Home and End, and type-ahead.
Touch targets are at least 30 by 30 pixels, and the panel follows the browser's default font size.
When keyboard focus lands on a page control under the launcher, the launcher steps aside until focus moves on (WCAG 2.4.11). It still covers its corner for mouse and touch users.
The widget never adjusts itself: text size, spacing, colors and filters apply to the page only, so the panel always looks and works the same.
It respects prefers-reduced-motion and Windows High Contrast (forced-colors), where its color filters switch off so the system colors win.

testing.title: Testing
testing.text: Every release runs in headless Chrome with axe-core (no violations allowed) and keyboard-only scripts, covering focus handling, reflow at 320 pixels and destroy(). Automated tests can't replace real screen readers, so a manual round with NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack and Windows High Contrast is asked for before major releases and recorded in docs/at-test-matrix.md.

keys: Open or close the panel. Also brings the widget back after “Hide widget”.
Close the panel (or the language list, or read mode); focus returns to where it was.
Move between controls. Focus stays inside the panel while it's open.
Press buttons, switches and profile cards; open and close sections.
Move between the options of a segmented choice.
Move through the language list; type a letter to jump to a language.
accessibility.note: The widget's own accessibility statement, with its known issues, is ACCESSIBILITY.md in the repository.

privacy.title: Privacy and storage
privacy.summary: What the widget stores, who can read it, and how to wait for consent.
privacy.intro: The widget runs entirely in the visitor's browser.

network.title: No network, no cookies
network.text: It makes no network requests, sets no cookies and has no analytics. The only request is the script itself, from your server or the CDN.

stored.title: What is saved
stored.text: With persist: true (the default) it uses two localStorage keys on your origin: a11yw-settings holds the visitor's adjustments and active profiles, and is removed when everything is back to default; a11yw-settings:lang holds the chosen language. storageKey changes the name.

readers.title: Who can read it
readers.text: Any script on the same origin (analytics, tag managers, session replay) can read those keys, the a11yw-* classes on html and the data-a11yw-fs attributes. Profile ids such as visionImpaired describe adjustments, but could be read as a hint about a visitor's needs. If you use session replay, mask the widget (.a11yw-root) and don't record the class names of html.

consent.title: Consent
consent.text: Whether saving preferences is strictly necessary (ePrivacy Art. 5(3)) and how GDPR applies is for your privacy team to decide. To store nothing, pass persist: false. To save only after consent, start with persist: false and turn it on once the visitor agrees.

security.title: Content Security Policy and SRI
security.summary: Run the widget under a strict CSP, and pin the CDN file with Subresource Integrity.
security.intro: The widget needs no unsafe-inline and no unsafe-eval.

csp.title: Content Security Policy
csp.text: It injects two style tags, so pass their nonce, and the large cursor is a data: SVG image. Leave out the CDN host when you bundle the package. CI runs the widget under default-src ''none'' with Trusted Types and fails on any violation.

sri.title: Subresource Integrity
sri.text: @1 on the CDN follows every 1.x release, so it can't carry an integrity hash. For production, pin an exact version with its hash: the browser refuses the file if the CDN ever serves something else. Compute the hash yourself or copy it from the file's page on jsdelivr.com, and update both when you upgrade.

trusted-types.title: Trusted Types
trusted-types.text: The widget builds its interface with createElement and never assigns HTML strings, so it works under require-trusted-types-for ''script'' with no policy of its own.

limitations.title: Limitations
limitations.summary: What the widget can't do, so you don't promise it.
limitations.intro: Read this before you describe the widget on your site or in your accessibility statement.

markup.title: It doesn't fix your site
markup.text: The widget changes how a page is displayed for one visitor. It doesn't make a site compliant with ADA, EAA, EN 301 549 or WCAG, and installing it is not a legal defence. Regulators act against products that claim otherwise, such as the FTC's 2025 order against accessiBe.
items: Missing alt text, form labels, headings, keyboard support and contrast in your own design still need fixing at the source.
Don't advertise the widget as a compliance solution, and don't present it as one in your accessibility statement.

reach.title: Where it can't reach
reach.text: Some parts of a page are out of the widget's reach.
items: Cross-origin iframe elements (embedded video, maps, payment forms) and closed shadow roots: browsers keep every script out of them. Same-origin iframes and open Shadow DOM are adjusted.
“Stop animations” stops CSS, script and SVG animations; GIFs, canvas and animation that scripts draw frame by frame keep moving.
The launcher steps aside when keyboard focus lands on a control under it (WCAG 2.4.11), but still covers its corner for mouse and touch users: keep that corner free, or move it with offset.

display.title: How adjustments display
display.text: Some adjustments trade precision for safety.
items: “Page zoom” uses CSS zoom, which doesn't trigger your media queries. Browser zoom reflows better: suggest it in your accessibility statement.
“Line spacing” sets a line height of 1.5 times the chosen percentage on all text.
Letter spacing is not applied to Arabic and other joined scripts (it would break the letters apart); word spacing still is.
Color modes override backgrounds and remove background images, except on form controls, links and buttons. Decorative icons drawn as background images elsewhere disappear.
Text size measures each element's size once. If your app later changes an element's font size through a class change, it keeps the earlier size until the page reloads.
Color adjustments apply to the screen only, not to printing.

browsers.title: Browser support
browsers.text: Chrome and Edge 120+, Firefox 126+ and Safari 16.4+ (desktop and mobile) get every feature; older versions lose single features, such as page zoom. CI runs the end-to-end tests in Chrome only; Firefox and Safari rest on feature support and manual testing.
